column3: Near-verbatim continuation: exclusive deity, praise, judgment, and return all recur in the same order.
Its hidden-and-public knowledge supplies the accountability field through which the focus's judgment operates.
Universal divine possession and the return of all affairs support the return clause, but omit praise and judgment.
Repeats exclusive deity and praise, then directs exclusive worship to the living God.
The same-surah repentance, faith, and righteous action show the accountable response to divine judgment.
Death followed by return to the Lord directly specifies the focus's final-return clause.
Pairs praise in this world and the Hereafter with divine possession and wisdom, closely extending the focus formula.
Immediate preceding context makes hidden and public human content subject to the Lord's knowledge before 28:70 declares His judgment.
The Quran's wisdom supports the focus's divine judgment, though it does not state the return or praise formula.
Exclusive deity is joined to justice and divine wisdom, strongly grounding the focus's sole authority.
Hidden and public speech lies within complete knowledge, a material accountability parallel to the focus.
Being called to God's Book for judgment illustrates human refusal of a judgment source, but remains a specific dispute scene.
Return to the true Master and His exclusive judgment closely restate the focus's final authority and return.
God's knowledge of secret and public acts provides the evidentiary horizon for the focus's judgment.
The afflicted confess belonging to God and returning to Him; the personal response is narrower than the focus's universal declaration.
Worship of the Creator is reasoned from the fact that all return to Him, directly joining devotion and return.
The lifeless false objects' ignorance of resurrection contrasts with the living God's authority over the final return.
It challenges corrupt human judging, contrasting it with the focus's declaration that judgment belongs to God.
Praise belongs to Him across heavens and earth, extending the focus's praise in the first life and the Hereafter.
Exclusive prostration and knowledge of concealed and declared matters support the focus's sole deity and accountable judgment.
Revealed truth authorizes just judgment among people, giving concrete expression to the focus's divine judgment.
God gives life and death and to Him all return, directly supplying the focus's return within divine sovereignty.
The layered refusal to hear the call only indirectly contrasts with submission to the sole God.
God alone opens and withholds mercy, a partial sovereignty parallel without the focus's return or praise.
Divine kingship, praise, and power over everything closely expand the focus's praise and sole authority.
Patience and righteous action with forgiveness do not materially clarify the focus's deity, judgment, praise, or return.
Pharaoh's denial that he will return directly negates the focus's final return and exposes its moral consequence.
Majesty belongs to God in heavens and earth and He is wise, supporting the authority behind the focus's judgment.
God knows what hearts conceal and what people declare, directly preparing the accountability implied by judgment.
The final mutual blame before the Lord alludes to return and reckoning, but not the focus's comprehensive authority.
The declaration that God is their Lord and to Him they return closely supports the return clause.
What is gathered from breasts supplies a final disclosure scene compatible with judgment after return.
The calf's inability to answer or control harm and benefit contrasts with the focus's living, ruling sole deity.
Created witnesses testify against people and all return to God, concretizing the focus's accountable final return.
The scattering of graves supplies the resurrection stage that precedes the focus's return and judgment.
The inability to proceed or return is a distinct earthly incapacity, only loosely related to final return.
It repeats exclusive deity and directs trust and repentance to Him, strongly echoing the focus's sole-God confession.
Repentance promises benefit and warns of a great day; it only indirectly anticipates the focus's judgment and return.
God's power to restore a person supports the possibility of the focus's final return, though the referent is less explicit.
Exclusive deity, universal possession, exhaustive knowledge, and unrivaled sovereignty strongly frame the focus's authority.
Knowledge of the warned event belongs to God, a narrow connection to divine knowledge rather than the focus's judgment formula.
Kingship belongs to God on that day and He judges between people, directly specifying the focus's judgment.
It joins rejection of rival worship with the explicit statement that judgment belongs only to God.
Return to God for notice of deeds supports accountability, but is framed within a parental-pressure command.
The Hereafter's superiority over the first life directly parallels the focus's two temporal domains.
Faith requires accepting the Messenger's judgment without inner resistance, concretely enacting submission to God's rule.
The Hereafter being better and more lasting clarifies the focus's praise across first life and Hereafter.
All affairs return to God, but the verse is primarily consolation after denial of messengers.
The first death and protection from punishment touch the first-life/Hereafter contrast without connecting judgment or praise.
Expectation of meeting the Lord and returning to Him supports the return clause, but remains a believer's disposition.
Joseph confesses God's care in this world and the Hereafter, providing a lived praise-and-afterlife parallel.
God inherits earth and all upon it and people return to Him, strongly expanding the focus's final ownership and return.
The deniers' claim of only a first death contradicts the focus's Hereafter horizon, but offers little positive development.
The matter is decided and all affairs return to God, connecting decisive judgment to the focus's return.
The mention of this world and the Hereafter occurs within a slander warning, without clarifying praise or judgment.
Their final destination is the Fire, a direct negative instance of the focus's return under divine judgment.
Praise belongs to God as Creator with unrestricted power, materially supporting the focus's praise and sovereignty.
Return after divorce is a legal reconciliation sense and only shares the root with the final return.
The claim of a single first death contrasts with the focus's Hereafter, but is merely a denial statement.
God commands trusts and just judgment among people, an explicit ethical outworking of His judgment.
Judgment belongs only to God and He tells the truth and decides best, closely matching the focus's exclusive judgment.
Life, death, renewed life, and return to God give a full creaturely sequence behind the focus's return.
Curse and humiliating punishment in this world and Hereafter offer a consequence setting but not the focus formula.
God judges disputed matters on the Day of Resurrection, directly applying the focus's divine judgment.
All in heavens and earth belong to Him and are obedient, supporting the comprehensive authority declared in the focus.
Return to God followed by full, unwronged repayment concretizes how the focus's judgment is enacted.
Judgment belongs only to God and trust is placed in Him, directly aligning exclusive authority with human reliance.
Return is to God, who is capable of everything, directly supports the focus's final return and authority.
The phrase 'former warnings' shares the first/earlier lexical field but not the focus's temporal praise contrast.
It exposes false partners and asks how people judge, reinforcing sole divine guidance and rightful judgment.
This-world/Hereafter loss and abiding Fire occur in a legal-conflict context, only broadly related to accountability.
The hypocrites' use of return to Medina is a different return sense, though divine honor corrects their false claim.
Near-verbatim exclusive-deity formula adds knowledge of unseen and seen, strongly extending the focus's sole God.
The warning against bribing judges concerns corrupt human legal practice, a limited contrast to divine judgment.
God originates and restores creation, then people return to Him, directly grounding the focus's final return.
Believers answer God's and the Messenger's summons to judge between them with hearing and obedience.
Exclusive deity and Lordship over east and west make Him the proper trustee, strongly supporting sole sovereignty.
Everyone returns to God to be informed of deeds; the personal-guidance instruction is narrower than the focus.
It repeats the exclusive-deity formula and makes trust in God its practical consequence.
The Lord decides between them by His judgment and is mighty and knowing, directly matching the focus's authority.
Near-verbatim exclusive-deity formula adds the most beautiful names, strongly reinforcing the focus's sole-God claim.
Their not returning describes moral incapacity, not the universal final return proclaimed in the focus.
Near-verbatim exclusive-deity formula unfolds kingship, holiness, protection, might, and transcendence over partners.
Return to God closes an exhortation on giving and divine provision; it supports accountability but not the full focus formula.
The concise exclusive-deity confession with the Living, Sustaining One directly reinforces the focus's identity claim.
The Book judges human disputes, a partial earthly analogue to divine judgment amid a broader history of disagreement.
God is deity in heaven and earth and is wise and knowing, expanding the universal scope behind His judgment.
God knows what is before and behind them and all affairs return to Him, strongly joining knowledge and return.
The true King and sole deity are exalted, closely grounding the focus's exclusive authority.
Denial of return is refuted by purposeful creation, directly explaining why the focus's return is not empty.
False security from God's plan warns of loss, but does not materially develop praise, judgment, or return.
Believers act with fearful hearts because they will return to their Lord, giving the focus's return an ethical effect.
Being left among later generations shares only the later/Hereafter lexical horizon, not the focus's meaning.
Revelation as an Arabic judgment and resistance to desires concretely express the binding authority named in the focus.
Fearfulness alone provides no identifiable connection to the focus's deity, praise, judgment, or return.
The brother awaits God's judgment and calls Him the best of judges, a localized human response to divine rule.
God's fuller knowledge and warning against self-purification only broadly support accountable judgment.
Patience for the Lord's judgment and praise of Him connect two focus themes, though in a prophetic endurance setting.
Returning after pilgrimage is a travel/legal sense, not the final return, and the verse does not develop judgment.
The gaze's return exposes the observer's limitation, a different return sense with only a distant accountability analogy.
Praise belongs to God as Lord of all worlds, establishing the focus's praise in universal sovereignty.
God is Master of the Day of Judgment, directly specifying the judgment declared in the focus.
Exclusive worship and reliance give the practical response to the focus's sole deity.
God grants and removes dominion and honors or humiliates whom He wills, strongly unfolding His ruling authority.
The sole deity will gather all people on the Day of Resurrection, directly joining exclusive deity and final return.
After the daytime term is completed, return is to God and He informs people of what they did.
It identifies God as Lord, sole deity, and Creator of all things, then commands worship of Him.
Each person bears his own burden, then returns to the Lord who discloses their differences.
As God originated people, so they return, directly supporting the focus's return as a creational completion.
The magicians confess that they will return to their Lord, giving the return clause a concrete confessional form.
The return of all is promised by God, who begins creation and repeats it to recompense justly.
At the final testing every soul learns what it sent ahead and is returned to its true Master.
A brief worldly enjoyment is followed by return to God and severe punishment, clarifying the first-life/Hereafter contrast.
The unseen of heavens and earth returns to God and all command belongs to Him; worship and trust follow.
God alone is Lord of heavens and earth; the verse exposes the incapacity of rivals through a sovereignty contrast.
God is self-sufficient and praiseworthy even if all humanity disbelieves, sharpening the independence of His praise.
Your God is one God; the verse directly supplies the focus's exclusive-deity declaration.
God commands that no two gods be taken, because He alone is God and alone is to be feared.
Whatever is in heavens and earth belongs to Him and enduring devotion is due to Him alone.
The hypothetical plurality of gods is refuted by the resulting rivalry for the Lord of the Throne.
Praise belongs to God without child or partner in dominion, directly extending the focus's praise and sole sovereignty.
God alone knows the unseen and shares His judgment with no one.
True protection, reward, and final outcome belong to God, the True, directly supporting His exclusive judgment.
The revealed message identifies the worshiped God as one and commands exclusive worship without association.
Every one comes to God individually on the Day of Resurrection, concretizing the focus's universal return.
God identifies Himself as the sole deity and commands worship and remembrance, directly paralleling the focus's confession.
God is the sole deity and encompasses everything in knowledge, expanding the focus's authoritative identity.
The impossibility of multiple gods in heaven and earth proves the singular sovereignty declared in the focus.
God is not questioned about what He does while creatures are questioned, clarifying the asymmetry of final judgment.
Every messenger receives the same sole-deity revelation and command for exclusive worship.
Jonah's confession, 'no deity but You,' is an intense personal enactment of the focus's exclusive deity.
God will judge the competing communities on the Day of Resurrection and is witness over all things.
Calling another god without proof leads to account before the Lord, directly opposing the focus's sole deity.
God's kingdom has no child or partner, and His measured creation establishes comprehensive sovereignty.
Trust the Ever-Living who does not die and glorify Him with praise, closely extending the focus's praise.
God alone is deity and Lord of the Mighty Throne, a concise direct parallel to the focus's sole deity.
The verse repeatedly asks whether any god is alongside God, exposing rival-deity claims through creation and provision.
Earth's stability, rivers, mountains, and seas are attributed to God alone against the question of any rival deity.
God answers the desperate, removes harm, and makes human beings successors; no rival deity shares this authority.
God guides through land and sea and sends mercy-bearing winds, again rejecting any deity alongside Him.
God originates and repeats creation, provides from heaven and earth, and rejects every alleged rival deity.
Immediate continuation: no deity other than God can bring light after perpetual night, applying exclusive deity to human need.
Immediate continuation: no deity other than God can bring night for rest after perpetual day.
Immediate continuation: night and day are divine mercy for rest, provision, and gratitude, directly extending praise in both temporal domains.
Immediate continuation: alleged partners are summoned for account before the sole God.
A witness from every community is brought and truth is shown to belong to God, extending the focus's judgment scene.
God creates, provides, causes death and life, then asks whether any alleged partners can do any of this.
Everything in heavens and earth belongs to God, who is self-sufficient and praiseworthy.
The Lord will judge people on the Day of Resurrection concerning their disputes.
Alleged partners possess no atom's weight in heavens or earth and have no share in God's authority.
Our Lord gathers all and then judges in truth, directly joining gathering, return, and judgment.
God alone creates and provides from heaven and earth; there is no deity but Him.
Human need and God's self-sufficiency and praiseworthiness give the focus's praise an explicit relational contrast.
All things are under God's dominion and all return to Him, a near-direct parallel to the focus's final authority.
Your God is one, directly repeating the focus's exclusive deity.
He is Lord of heavens, earth, and all between them, grounding universal sovereignty.
Sincere religion belongs exclusively to God, directly applying the focus's sole deity to worship.
All intercession belongs to God; His is the dominion of heavens and earth, and to Him people return.
God knows the unseen and seen and judges His servants in their differences, directly expanding the focus's judgment.
Rejection when God alone is called and belief when partners are associated makes judgment belong to the Exalted Great.
God judges with truth while those invoked besides Him judge nothing.
The return is to God, and the transgressors are companions of the Fire, specifying judgment after return.
God is Lord and Creator of all things; there is no deity but Him.
God fashioned the earth and heaven, formed humanity, provided good things, and is blessed as Lord of all worlds.
Doubt about meeting the Lord is answered by His encompassing knowledge, supporting final return and accountability.
Whatever people differ over, its judgment belongs to God; He is the Lord upon whom one relies and turns.
The path is God's, to whom all in heavens and earth belongs and to whom all matters return.
There is no deity but God; He gives life and death and is Lord of ancestors and descendants.
Each soul is recompensed for its deeds and all are returned to their Lord.
God created heavens and earth in truth so every soul may be recompensed without injustice.
God gives life and death, then gathers all people for the Day of Resurrection beyond doubt.
All praise belongs to God, Lord of heavens, earth, and all worlds.
The rhetorical question rejects the possibility of any deity besides God and declares His transcendence over association.
God owns the dominion of heavens and earth, gives life and death, and has power over all things.
The dominion of heavens and earth belongs to Him and all matters return to God.
God is Creator, Originator, and Fashioner; the most beautiful names and universal glorification complete the focus's praise.
Blessed is He in whose hand is all dominion and who has power over everything.
God created human faculties and dispersed humanity, then gathers all to Himself.
God is One, the clearest concise affirmation of the focus's exclusive deity.
God's absolute self-sufficiency explains why praise, judgment, and return cannot belong to any dependent rival.
